Our study provides a systematic assessment of the effects of ant activities on SOC storage and CO2 emissions from multiple perspectives by comparing ant nest soils with reference soils without nests. It advanced our understanding of ant involvement in the terrestrial carbon cycle. However, the study still had several limitations, such as insufficient sample sizes for studies in regions rich in ant diversity, that is, arid regions in Africa, South America, and Australia39,57 (Supplementary Fig. 2). Combined with findings that ants have larger relative effects on soil carbon in resource-poor ecosystems, this may underestimate the global carbon engineering effects of ants. Arid ecosystems are frequently characterized by irregular pulse rainfall events, which substantially modulate soil carbon changes. In addition, our dataset lacks reports on sampling dates relative to rainfall events and does not provide detailed precipitation data on ant carbon effects. We emphasize the importance of considering irregular pulse rainfall events in future related studies. All studies included in our meta-analysis failed to quantify net carbon fluxes integrating both fixation and emission processes. Consequently, we could not directly assess the net carbon balance influenced by ants from the current dataset. Future studies should consider the overall effect of ants on the carbon cycle and standardize measurement protocols to determine whether ant activities turn soils into net carbon sources or sinks under contrasting environmental conditions. Given the lack of appropriate data, we could not quantify the differences in carbon effects across various sampling locations within an ant nest. Future studies should use the whole-nest sampling and assessment rather than site-specific sampling approaches to accurately quantify the ecological effects of ants on entire nests. This is necessary to estimate the direction of ant effects on soil carbon. Previous studies have assessed global ant abundance, biomass, and distribution8. However, ant effects are more confined to the nest area, and colony size and body size may be key factors effecting the intensity of ant-induced soil disturbance. Our results revealed that ant respiration accounted for 52% of CO2 emissions from ant nests, and the effect of ants on soil carbon is also correlated with body size. Therefore, studies of soil fauna (including ants) within nests should estimate colony size to enable a more detailed assessment of taxon-specific quantitative differences in soil carbon effects.

Taken together, previous studies and our results indicate that ants aid carbon storage via increased SOC formation and accumulation, particularly in arid regions with poor soil quality (low initial SOC), where ants create hotspots of SOC transformation. However, ant activity accelerates CO2 emissions, which may partially offset the positive effects on SOC accumulation. Moreover, compared with other environmental factors, the functional traits of ants have greater explanatory power for the changes in SOC storage and CO2 emissions. Species determine ant survival strategies, while nesting strategies and primary food sources determine the magnitude and direction of ant carbon effects. Given that ant functional traits are largely shaped by climate, we highlight that shifts in these strategies amid intensifying climate change could profoundly alter soil carbon dynamics.

We compiled a global dataset on the effects of ants on soil carbon based on literature searches (ending on June 2024) using the Web of Science (http://isiknowledge.com) and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (http://www.cnki.net) databases. This search was performed from February to June 2024 using the following search terms: (ants OR ant) AND (soil organic carbon OR SOC OR TC OR TOC OR soil C OR soil organic matter OR SOM OR greenhouse gas OR GHG OR soil respiration OR CO2 efflux OR CO2 emissions OR carbon dioxide emissions OR N2O emissions OR nitrous oxide emissions OR N2O flux OR CH4 emissions OR methane emissions OR methane flux). We also reviewed references cited in relevant doctoral and master’s theses. To minimize selection bias, we included only studies that met the following criteria: (1) assessed the effects of ant nests on SOC and/or GHG emissions; (2) explicitly reported the experimental ecosystems, nest status, experiment environment types (e.g., field or laboratory), and ant species; and (3) defined and compared control and treatment groups, where the control comprised soils without ant activity or nesting and the treatment comprised soils from the same study that contained ant nests or associated biogenic structures (e.g., mounds, nests, and refuse piles). Ultimately, our analysis was based on 2232 observations gleaned from 136 studies (including peer-reviewed articles, theses, and reports). A flowchart illustrating the literature search process and its results is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1. A full list of manuscripts included in this meta-analysis is available in the Figshare deposition.

We extracted and stored these data: mean values of SOC and/or GHG emissions for the control treatment and the experimental treatment in each study, along with their standard deviation (SD) and sample sizes (n). For studies that did not report an SD or standard error (SE), we estimated the SD values as SE * √n when the SE was available. When error bars were unspecified, we assumed they represented the SE rather than the SD. If both the SD and SE were missing, we conservatively estimated SD as 1/10 of the mean for the corresponding treatment group in this study58. This conservative method was applied to approximately 14% of SOC effect sizes (48 of 432) and 15% of CO2 emission effect sizes (31 of 203), while the remainder was based on reported statistical data. Data extractions from tables or figures were done using GetData Graph Digitizer software v.2.26 (http://getdata-graphdigitizer.com/).

The extracted variables included SOC storage, ST, soil water content, BD, and pH; sand, silt, and clay content; total nitrogen (TN), the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio (C/N), and readily oxidizable carbon (ROC); ammonium (NH4⁺) and nitrate (NO3⁻) concentrations in soil solution; microbial biomass carbon (MBC); fungal, bacterial, and actinomycete abundance, and fluxes of CO2, N2O, and CH4. In addition, we recorded the longitude and latitude information of the study sites, local mean annual precipitation (MAP), and local MAT, initial soil pH level, and initial SOC storage of the study sites. Initial soil pH and SOC storage represented control soils unaffected by ant activity or corresponding undisturbed soil properties at the study sites. To maintain the accuracy of site-specific conditions, these variables reported in the original studies were adopted when available, which better represent the experimental environment. When these variables were unavailable, missing climate data (32%) were obtained from the WorldClim database (http://www.worldclim.org/, resolution: 30 s)59, while missing values for initial SOC (13%) and soil pH (43%) were extracted from the Soil Grid datasets with 30 s spatial resolution60. Aridity index data were retrieved from the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Climate Database v.361.The aridity index is defined as the ratio of annual precipitation to potential evapotranspiration, with higher values indicating a more humid climate (e.g., AI ≥ 0.65 typically indicates a humid climate61), whereas lower values indicate greater aridity. Owing to high collinearity (|r| > 0.7; Supplementary Fig. 2) between absolute latitude, MAP, and other predictors in specific data subsets, we excluded these two predictors from model analyses. Study sites were categorized into specific biomes using their MAT and MAP data based on the Whittaker classification system. When geographic coordinates were not available, we determined them using ArcGIS (ESRI, CA, USA) based on location descriptions in the original studies. Finally, we also recorded a suite of study characteristics: biogeographic region (tropical, subtropical, and temperate), ecosystem (cropland, desert, forest, grassland, mining area, wetland), ant species (subfamily, genus), nesting strategy (above mound mineral, above mound thatch, surface detritus, and subterranean nest), and primary diet (fungivore, granivore, honeydew, omnivorous, and predatory/saprophagous). For studies reporting species information, we compiled body size traits for further analysis. The maximum head width (in millimeters) of worker ants was obtained from the GlobalAnts database62 or measured it using images with scales provided by AntWeb63. Given that head width typically exhibits stable scaling relationships with body mass/biomass, we determined that using head width as a body size proxy is reasonable5.

We used multilevel mixed-effects models with the rma.mv function in the metafor package67. Observations nested in studies (~1| reference/obs) served as the random effect to account for non-independence in the data (i.e., multiple observations within a single study). To optimize the model structure, we compared different random effect configurations based on the Bayesian Information Criterion to balance model complexity and fit quality68. The final model retained a nested random-effects structure (~1| reference/obs), partitioning variance between studies and among effect sizes within studies, thereby effectively controlling hierarchical dependence (Supplementary Table 14).

For studies reporting multiple treatment groups compared with the same control group, we calculated the log-response ratio for each treatment relative to the common control. However, this approach inherently violated the assumption of statistical independence among effect sizes, as multiple effect sizes share variance from the same control group69. To resolve this dependency, we constructed variance covariance (VCV) matrices for each dataset following the methodology of Lajeunesse65. These VCV matrices explicitly modeled the covariance arising from the repeated use of the same control group in within-study comparisons, thereby eliminating potential biases stemming from non-independent effect sizes.

We used the ranger package for random forest models to assess the contributions of multiple variables70. The model analysis considered the following predictors: (1) climate factors (aridity index, MAT); (2) soil properties (initial SOC storage, initial pH); (3) ant species; (4) nesting strategy; (5) primary diet; and (6) ecosystem type. For the CO2 emission analysis, we also incorporated (7) experimental type (field or laboratory) as a predictor to evaluate the possible moderating effect of the experimental design used. Field experiments typically involved gas flux measurements using experimental chambers placed over active ant nests, a process including the physiological respiration of ants. Laboratory experiments, however, involved collecting soil from ant nests in the field and bringing it back to the lab for soil respiration measurements, thereby excluding the respiration of the ants themselves. This experimental design allowed us to distinguish between soil CO2 emission sources including ant respiration and those excluding it. We employed the plspm package for partial least squares structural equation modeling (PL-SEM) to elucidate the regulatory pathways influencing the effects of ants on SOC and GHG emissions. For categorical variables in the model (i.e., ecosystem type, ant functional strategy), we first preprocessed them using dummy variable encoding (generating k-1 numerical dummy variables for a variable with k levels, selecting an ecologically meaningful level as the reference group)71. Based on this, the path coefficients of categorical variables could be interpreted as the effect bias of the target group (i.e., each level not in the reference group) compared with the reference group. These coefficients not only reveal the direction of differences (positive/negative) but also quantify the magnitude of these differences through standardized coefficient values. This directly reflects the specific variations in the effects of ants on SOC storage or CO2 emissions across various contexts (e.g., different ecosystem types or nesting strategies).

While constructing mixed-effects models, we incorporated both linear and quadratic terms for continuous variables. We calculated AICc, and AICc (corrected for small sample sizes) to determine which model fit better. If the AICc value was lower, we considered the model with the lower AICc value to be superior to the other model (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). For categorical factors, analyses were conducted without an intercept to obtain parameter estimates representing the mean effect sizes per level. All parameter estimates were reported for best models run with REML (restricted maximum likelihood). The heterogeneity explained by the moderators in each independent meta-regression was assessed using the test of moderators (QM). To Increase result accuracy, subgroups with small sample sizes (n < 5) were excluded in subsequent subgroup analyses.

Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s tests, with accuracy (standard error, SE) included as a covariate in the rma.mv function72. These tests indicated that the overall response ratio (RR) for SOC was robust, albeit with a slight potential publication bias for CO2 (Supplementary Fig. 4). We then used Rosenberg’s fail-safe numbers to assess the robustness of results against publication bias73. We found that only one ant effect (CH4 emissions, P = 0.40) yielded a non-significant and small fail-safe number, while all other models produced large fail-safe numbers reaching statistical significance (P < 0.05; Supplementary Table 2). This indicated that the reported soil engineering effects of ants has strong robustness to publication bias.

A leave-one-study-out sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess the robustness of the pooled effect size and identify the potential influence of individual studies on the overall results67. We sequentially excluded each individual study from the full dataset, and then reran a multilevel mixed-effects model identical to the main analysis structure using the remaining studies (Supplementary Figs. 15 and 16). The pooled effect size and its 95% confidence interval (95% CI) from each reanalysis were subsequently compared with the main analysis results. Results showed that regardless of which individual study was excluded, the direction of the pooled effect (positive or negative impact of ant nests on SOC or CO2) remained consistent with the primary analysis, and the recalculated 95% CI for the pooled effect size did not exhibit significant shifts. This indicated robustness of our overall findings (Supplementary Figs. 15 and 16).

We assessed the heterogeneity in nest soil effects across studies by calculating the I2 statistics67. We found extremely high total heterogeneity across studies for most ecosystem traits (91–100%; Supplementary Table 2), with inter-study heterogeneity accounting for the majority (47–75%). This confirmed the necessity of investigating how ant functional traits or environmental variations modify the effects of nest soils on carbon accumulation and mineralization. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (v. 4.5.1) (https://www.rproject.org). The maps shown in Fig. 1a, b were generated using the geographic coordinates reported in the original studies, with world boundaries rendered using the maps package and plotting performed with ggplot2. Supplementary Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 3a and 14a were generated in ArcGIS using the Copernicus Climate Change Service land-cover dataset (version 2.1.1)74.
